opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and honestly some of them are quite understandable.

The first is historical. Many people in robotics have been burned by simulation before. Ten years ago, you'd train something in a simulator, it looked beautiful, and then you put it on a real robot and it completely fell apart. The so-called sim-to-real gap was very real, especially for contact-rich manipulation: friction, deformation, soft objects, cables, cloth. So there's a kind of scar tissue in the community. When people hear "synthetic data," they remember all those failures.

The second reason is the success of large language models. Their lesson seems to be: collect massive amounts of real data, scale it up, and intelligence emerges. So many people naturally map that onto robotics: just teleoperate, collect huge amounts of real-world robot data, and scaling will solve everything. Under that narrative, synthetic data looks like a shortcut, or even a distraction.

But I think that analogy misses something important. Language data was already there. Humans had written it on the internet for decades, essentially for free. Robot action data doesn't exist at that scale. Every hour of real teleoperation costs money, hardware, people, and time. And even if you spend a lot, the diversity is limited: the same labs, the same tables, the same few hundred objects. You can't easily get millions of scenes, lighting conditions, object geometries, and failure cases from real data alone.

That's where I believe synthetic data is essential. Simulation and rendering have advanced dramatically, along with procedural generation and now generative models for assets. For many tasks, especially grasping, navigation, and a large part of pick-and-place, we've shown you can train mostly or even entirely in simulation and achieve strong zero-shot transfer to the real world. The key is that you don't need the simulator to be perfect. You need enough diversity and randomization that the real world just looks like another sample from the distribution.

The third reason, if I'm being frank, is incentives. If your company's competitive moat is a large real-data collection operation, you're naturally inclined to argue real data is the only path. And synthetic data pipelines are actually hard to build well. They require graphics, physics, and learning expertise all at once. So it's easier to say "it doesn't work" than to invest years making it work.

My own view isn't that real data is useless. Real data is very valuable for fine-tuning, for evaluation, and for the long tail that simulation can't yet capture well. But I think the foundation, the bulk of the pretraining for embodied intelligence, should come from synthetic data. Otherwise, I really don't see how we reach the data scale needed for a general-purpose robot within any reasonable timeframe or cost.

r001.rationale: The response links opposition to companies whose competitive advantage is real-data collection, but does not attribute it to a commercial need to sell robots.

r002.rationale: It does not say that robotics practitioners who oppose synthetic data use it themselves.

r003.rationale: It discusses the sim-to-real gap and the value of diversity and randomization, but does not state that effective synthetic-data use requires systematically addressing those gaps throughout the robotic system.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the opposition comes from a few places, and honestly some of it is reasonable.

The first is the sim-to-real gap. For years, the dominant experience in robotics was that you'd train something beautifully in simulation and it would fall apart the moment it touched a real object. Friction, contact, deformable things, lighting, sensor noise: simulators got these wrong, and people got burned. So there's a kind of institutional memory in the field that says "synthetic data looks good on paper but doesn't transfer." That memory is earned, and I don't dismiss it.

The second reason is more about what people think "data" means. If you come from the vision or language side, you think of data as something you scrape and scale. Robotics people think of data as something you collect with a physical robot, because the whole point is the physical interaction. So when someone says "we'll just generate it," it sounds like a shortcut around the hard part, around the actual physics. There's an almost cultural reaction to that.

The third is a mismatch of time horizon. Teleoperation and real-robot collection give you results you can see this month. Building a simulation pipeline that's good enough to generalize is a long investment: assets, physics, domain randomization, rendering, and then you still have to validate on real hardware. For a lab or a startup under pressure, real data feels safer even if it doesn't scale.

Where I disagree is on the conclusion. The sim-to-real gap is a problem to be engineered down, not a law of nature. If you look at what's worked in grasping and in dexterous manipulation, a lot of it comes from millions of synthetic trials you simply could not collect physically. Real data is expensive, it's limited to the scenes you have, and it's biased by the operators. Synthetic data gives you coverage: rare objects, rare poses, failure cases, things you'd never see in a thousand hours of teleop. And once the model learns from that breadth, a small amount of real data closes the remaining gap much more efficiently.

So I'd frame it this way: it's not synthetic versus real. The question is what each kind of data is good for. Simulation is for scale and coverage. Real data is for calibration to the world. People who oppose synthetic data are usually reacting to the bad version of it, where you train in sim and pray. That's not the proposal anymore.

r001.rationale: The response attributes opposition to bad sim-to-real experiences, beliefs about physical data, and time horizons; it does not mention a commercial need to sell robots.

r002.rationale: The response says robotics practitioners favor collecting real data, but does not say that those who oppose synthetic data use it themselves.

r003.rationale: It says the sim-to-real gap must be engineered down and identifies issues across physics, contact, lighting, sensors, rendering, and validation on real hardware.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the skepticism comes from the gap between what looks realistic and what actually behaves realistically. In robotics, you have to interact with the world. An image can look convincing, but if the friction, contact, or motion is wrong, the robot may learn something that doesn’t transfer.

So when people push back on synthetic data, they’re often asking a reasonable question: does this actually improve performance on a real robot? If you only show results in simulation, you haven’t answered that.

But I don’t think that means synthetic data is inherently ineffective. It means we have to be precise about what we use it for. You can use it to introduce variation, cover situations that are difficult to collect, and then use real data to ground the learning. The useful question is where synthetic data helps, how much real data you still need, and whether the combination works better in the real world.

r001.rationale: It attributes skepticism to concerns about realism and real-robot performance, not opponents’ commercial need to sell robots.

r002.rationale: It does not say that practitioners who oppose synthetic data use it themselves.

r003.rationale: It mentions grounding learning with real data and checking transfer, but does not state that effective use requires systematically addressing simulation-to-reality gaps throughout the robotic system.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of the skepticism comes from the gap between what looks realistic and what is actually useful for a robot. You can generate a beautiful image, but that doesn’t mean the contact, friction, or object behavior is right. And those details matter when you’re trying to manipulate something.

So if you train on synthetic data and it doesn’t transfer to the real world, it’s natural to become skeptical. But I wouldn’t frame it as synthetic data versus real data. The question is: which parts of the task can synthetic data teach effectively, and where do you need real experience? Ultimately, you have to show that it improves the robot’s performance in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response attributes skepticism to gaps between realistic-looking data and useful robot behavior; it does not mention opponents’ commercial need to sell robots.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that practitioners who oppose synthetic data also use it themselves.

r003.rationale: It mentions sim-to-real transfer problems and examples such as contact and friction, but does not state that effective use requires systematically addressing gaps throughout the robotic system.
